content: When a poison center is newly established and receives only a limited number of inquiries, having a clinical toxicology unit may not be immediately necessary. However, as the center grows and develops, establishing such a unit should become a priority. Some poison centers include a clinical toxicology unit that specializes in treating poisoned patients. These patients may either be directly admitted to the unit or transferred from other hospitals for advanced care. A dedicated clinical toxicology unit plays a critical role in managing and treating poisoning cases. It enhances the identification of toxic substances, evaluates their effects, investigates the mechanisms and kinetics of various toxic actions, and assesses new diagnostic and therapeutic techniques. Typically, clinical toxicology units are staffed by specially trained nurses and medical toxicologists. In some cases, nurses may also handle poison-related inquiries. It is essential to ensure adequate staffing to maintain the quality of both clinical care and the advice provided to the public. One significant advantage of combining treatment facilities for poisoned patients with a poisons information center is the opportunity for clinical staff to gain hands-on experience in managing poisoning cases. This integration helps build their expertise and knowledge. Additionally, it provides training opportunities for poisons information specialists, who can participate in case reviews. The collaboration between information centers and treatment services facilitates the continuous updating and expansion of knowledge on diagnosing and treating local poisoning cases. It also encourages detailed follow-up of patients and stimulates essential research in human toxicology and patient management. Access to laboratory services for toxicological analyses and biomedical investigations is crucial for diagnosing, assessing, and treating certain types of poisoning. This is particularly important when differentiating poisoning from other diseases. Clinical units treating poisoned patients must have access to a toxicology laboratory, as rapid analytical data may be required to guide diagnosis and therapeutic decisions, such as the use of antidotes or enhanced elimination techniques, and to determine the endpoint of such therapies. After large-scale chemical events or novel exposures, toxicology laboratories must be capable of quickly processing samples and identifying the chemicals involved. Toxicology laboratory services can be cost-effective, as a single laboratory can serve a large population or territory. These services can reduce healthcare costs by confirming whether a patient has been exposed to or poisoned by a substance and whether specific treatment is necessary. They can also help avoid unnecessary treatments, overtreatment, or prolonged hospital stays. Laboratory analyses are also valuable for monitoring the effectiveness of treatments. Toxicology laboratories support research, such as determining the pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination) of toxicants. They also generate data useful for pharmacovigilance, toxicovigilance, and surveillance, as well as for the early identification of new public health threats. At a minimum, a toxicology laboratory should be able to identify, characterize, and ideally quantify toxic substances in biological fluids. The capacity to analyze other tissues, such as hair or nails, and environmental samples may be developed later or outsourced to other specialized laboratories, such as forensic or environmental labs. Given the importance of laboratories in identifying and confirming toxic exposures, access to a toxicology laboratory is considered a core capacity under the International Health Regulations (IHR). However, in many lowand middle-income countries, there are very few toxicology laboratories capable of analyzing clinical samples for a wide range of toxic substances. In such cases, combining clinical analytical toxicology services with those for forensic medicine, occupational toxicology, therapeutic drug monitoring, food contaminants, substance abuse, or veterinary toxicology may be necessary. Developing laboratory networks and mutual assistance agreements should be part of preparedness planning. For example, after a large-scale chemical or mass poisoning incident, local toxicological laboratories may lack the capacity to conduct all necessary analyses and may require assistance from other laboratories, including those in neighboring countries. Such arrangements can also benefit low-resource countries by ensuring access to rarely required toxicological assays. Laboratory networks can support the development of new analytical methods, training, and the provision of reference standards. A laboratory should have sufficient staff and equipment to conduct essential analyses for poisoning cases in the country or region. The proximity of laboratories to poisons information centers and treatment services can promote interdisciplinary collaboration. Poisons information centers may also engage in other activities, such as toxicovigilance, which involves monitoring and analyzing poisoning cases to identify trends, populations at risk, and emerging hazards. This function allows poison centers to alert public health authorities and other stakeholders to take preventive and regulatory measures. For example, a poison center may identify a surge in poisoning cases linked to a newly introduced product, harmful use of psychoactive substances, or contamination of pharmaceutical preparations. By communicating these findings, poison centers contribute to public health and safety. Prevention of poisoning is a key goal for public health and chemical safety. Poison center staff can use their data and expertise to alert authorities and manufacturers to high-risk situations, enabling the implementation of preventive measures. These measures may include regulatory actions, such as requiring precautionary labeling, child-resistant packaging, or the withdrawal of hazardous products from the market. Poison centers can also assess the impact of these measures on poisoning incidence and severity. Direct communication with the public through mass and social media, brochures, and educational activities is another aspect of prevention. Campaigns may be seasonal, such as those addressing carbon monoxide poisoning in winter, or targeted at specific groups, such as new parents or gardeners. A notable example of a successful prevention intervention is the introduction of child-resistant packaging in the USA during the 1970s, which significantly reduced accidental ingestions among children. Poisons information centers also play a critical role in chemical incident preparedness and response. They provide expertise in diagnosing and managing exposures to a wide range of substances and maintain databases on chemical toxicity. Poison centers can advise first responders and public health authorities during chemical incidents, whether they involve industrial spills, contaminated products, or deliberate chemical releases. Their involvement in preparedness planning strengthens their role in incident response. Coordination of antidote and antivenom supplies is another important function of poison centers. They can evaluate the requirements for these treatments, advise on cost-effective stocking strategies, and maintain inventories to ensure availability during emergencies. Some poison centers act as centralized holding centers for rarely used antidotes and antivenoms, dispatching them as needed. Teaching and training are essential activities for poison centers. They provide education to medical practitioners, first responders, and helpline staff, building a cadre of trained medical toxicologists. Poison centers may also engage in public education, such as teaching poisoning prevention in schools or to new parents. Finally, poison centers are uniquely positioned to conduct and publish research based on their data. This research can identify trends, evaluate prevention measures, and study the circumstances of poisoning to inform public health interventions. Findings should be regularly published in peer-reviewed journals, and staff should actively participate in national and international conferences to share their expertise.
